extracted.intended_audience: criminalists, judges, lawyers, police investigators, forensic examiners (readers concerned with reliability of witness testimony)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating the reliability of sensory witness testimony (vision, hearing, touch) in criminal cases by identifying causes of illusions, recommended tests, and when to call experts. Emphasizes factors that distort perception and procedures to detect or compensate for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strangeness_of_experience_makes_perceptions_unreliable
rubrics_metrics.description: “From the moment a thing becomes strange to an individual his perceptions are no longer reliable, it is doubtful whether he knows what he has really experienced before his world became strange to him.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an object or situation becomes 'strange' to a witness, sensory illusions and uncanny sensations can substitute for real perception; the one may cause the other and magnify it until the affair is unrecognizable. Treat such testimonies as suspect and probe for the onset of strangeness or unease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Witnesses_may_not_report_feeling_ill_at_ease
rubrics_metrics.description: “Few people are unwilling to confess that they felt ill at ease, that perhaps they do not even know it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because witnesses often do not acknowledge or recognize discomfort or nervousness that affects perception, investigators should not rely on spontaneous self-reporting of these states and should instead ask targeted questions or seek corroborating indicators of unease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical_illusions_from_disease_or_intoxication
rubrics_metrics.description: Diseased excitability of the retina and effects of narcotics cause optical illusions (e.g., morphine fiends and cocaine victims have strong tendencies to optical illusions). Himly: 'in the diseased excitability of the retina every color is a tone higher.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lay observers cannot reliably detect these conditions. If a witness might be diseased, intoxicated, or otherwise physiologically altered, call a physician or treat the testimony as potentially distorted (color shifts, inverted substitutions, altered form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical_illusions_from_retina_movement_touch_disruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Optical illusions occur when communication between the retina, sense of movement, and sense of touch is interrupted, or when retinal image changes are not reduced to movements of body/eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask witnesses how they observed something (fixed glance vs following it). Where speed, size, or motion is contested, probe whether the observer tracked the object or had only a fixed glance—this affects judgments of speed and location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception_distortion_when_observer_is_in_motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever we ourselves move quickly we make false judgments of size, distance, and even color (examples: train makes objects seem too near/smaller; bicycle observations increase such illusions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially skeptical of testimony obtained while the witness was in rapid motion (on foot, bicycle, or train). Reconstruct vantage and motion to evaluate likely distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fechner_and_movement_effects_on_apparent_motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fechner: things on the ground appear to run when we ride by them rapidly; viewing swift-moving water from a low bridge may make the bridge seem to swim upstream.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these known perceptual effects when assessing witness descriptions of relative motion and direction—queries should seek whether observed motion could be an effect of observer movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination_can_animate_and_alter_static_percepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination may cause static objects to be seen as moving or altered (examples: corpse appearing to move as it thawed; ink-blot seen as a drop of water reflecting a window; tailor's scissors composed of accidental reflections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should consider that strong imagination can persistently create false perceptions even when witness is later told the truth; ask witnesses whether they moved closer or relied on indirect impressions and attempt to elicit conditions that encouraged imaginative elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge_of_impossibility_can_suppress_illusion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Only when I thought vigorously that such a thing could not possibly be in my room did it disappear.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Awareness and deliberate checking can eliminate some illusions; testing a witness's prior beliefs and whether they inspected the object can indicate susceptibility to sustained illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect_vision_is_approximate_and_permits_imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: “In order to see correctly we must look straight and fully at the object. Looking askance gives only an approximate image, and permits the imagination free play.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a witness saw an object only peripherally or indirectly, treat identification and detail claims as tentative. Whenever possible require direct fixation or reenactment of the view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathetic_induction_and_collective_perception
rubrics_metrics.description: When one object in a complex scene appears correct the correctness 'passes' to the whole collection (the public's sense is 'sympathetically inductive'), e.g., stage effects where plastic foreground objects induce perceived materiality in painted background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group viewing and contextual cues can bias individual perception; take individual statements separately and account for social/collective induction when many witnesses report similar but possibly induced impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatrical_stage_techniques_produce_strong_illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene painters 'proceed according to experience' producing impressions (rose arbor, Battle of Gravelotte panoramas) that convince varied audiences though only certain characteristics are emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that realistic arrangements of salient cues can cause observers to 'fill in' the rest; investigate whether foreground cues or staging could have produced a false holistic impression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hasty_first_impressions_often_lead_to_false_conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: A hasty view can lead to radically false first conceptions (board fence with moss seen as moss-covered rock leading to seeing a cliff; a single window perceived as many and so the inn as a mansion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First impressions should be treated with suspicion, especially if the witness did not examine the scene again directly. Corroboration and later inspection are necessary to correct initial inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience-based 'natural_standard'_can_distort_photographic_truth
rubrics_metrics.description: We know by experience how big a head is and ordinarily see relations of size in proportion; on a photograph unusual perspectives (e.g., large boots and small head) appear ludicrous though they may be accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses will report what experience suggests rather than what direct perception showed; do not assume photographic or measurement evidence is at fault if it contradicts testimony based on experiential standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irradiation_and_background_affect_perceived_size_and_color
rubrics_metrics.description: The appearance of dark bodies as covered with rays by adjacent luminosities; white square on black ground appears larger than identical black square on white ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When size or color matters, consider object color, background, and lighting (irradiation) as causes of misestimation; reconstruct lighting/background where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditory_illusions_are_frequent_and_critical
rubrics_metrics.description: “Incorrect hearing is much more frequent than incorrect seeing... real acoustic illusions are closely connected with auditory misapprehension and a distinction between these two can not be rigorously drawn.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat heard evidence with caution; examine possibilities of echo, pitch confusion, repetition, false coincidence, and environmental acoustics when evaluating hearing-based testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific_examples_of_auditory_confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples where 'Frozen' was heard as 'Oh, my,' and 'Herr Maier' as 'mamma' at certain locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete auditory confusion examples to show how distinct words may be misheard depending on location and acoustics; where possible, recreate the auditory conditions to test plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual_variation_in_hearing_acuity
rubrics_metrics.description: There are hyper-auditive individuals (musicians, young girls, nervous persons) and normal/abnormal variation in power of hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess witness hearing ability (musician, age, illness) and, when feasible, perform comparative tests under the same conditions rather than assuming homogeneous auditory capability among witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental_and_weather_effects_on_hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Difference between hearing in noisy day vs quiet night; influence of resonance, pitch, echo, absorption, temperature, atmospheric pressure, colds, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recreate or account for environmental acoustic conditions in evaluating auditory testimony; adjust credibility if conditions would have altered perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diseases_and_states_require_medical_examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory illusions occur in fever, hysteria, nervousness, alcoholism, diseases of the ear, etc.; some conditions are not apparent to laymen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call a physician when a witness’s hearing might be impaired by disease or abnormal states; medical testimony may be necessary to determine whether perception was pathological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotonous_sounds_and_sleepiness_cause_reduplication_or_miscounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Counting clock beats in sleepiness regularly yields one too many; double beat of the hammer (hearing a blow again when ears are closed briefly); monotonous murmur can produce perceived voices or music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious of timing evidence and perceptions arising during fatigue or monotony; consider physiological mechanisms (Eustachian tube action, reflections) that could create spurious repetitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonlinear_effects_on_sound_intensity_and_number
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty distinguishing intensity or number of simultaneous sounds (e.g., male choir of 400 not essentially louder than 200; one locust unheard, thousand locusts heard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume linear relationships in perceived loudness or count of sources; use controlled tests or corroboration to assess claims about numbers or loudness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions_of_direction_of_sound_are_common
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people cannot reliably distinguish the source and direction of street music, rolling wagons, or bells; even animals are subject to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat directional claims about sound with skepticism unless tested under similar conditions; attempts to train direction-finding may still fail due to accidental influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observations_require_corroboration_by_parallel_consistent_evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: “Every observation is not proof but means of proof, and that it may be trusted only when it is confirmed by many parallel actions which are really consistent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always seek independent corroboration; even after doing all within human power mistakes remain possible, so rely on multiple consistent lines of evidence for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touch_is_valuable_but_unreliable_if_sole_basis
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of touch is a control of sight but must never be depended upon when it is the sole instrument of perception; statements based entirely on touch are unreliable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require visual confirmation for tactile-only claims where possible. Be cautious of wound-location/time/manner descriptions based solely on touch—victims misattribute pain and order of injuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pain_and_wound_sensation_misattribute_time_and_cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Wounded persons often misidentify the time/manner of wounds (e.g., a long shallow cut causing burning while a deep stab causes the feeling of a heavy blow; later pain affects memory of which wound occurred when).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obtain medical records, call surgeons/physicians, and avoid relying on a victim’s subjective sequencing of pains without medical corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tabulation_and_medical_expertise_for_wound_reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Best practice: tabulation and accurate description of wounds (place, size, form), victim's feeling at moment, consequences, and explanatory observations to compare subjective feelings with objective wounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect structured, tabulated data about wounds and involve medical examiners to distinguish true subjective feelings from later learned identifications; use this as a psychophysical dataset to generalize rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactile_illusions_and_difficulty_judging_weights_and_points
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments show illusions of pressure (open compasses pressed on skin felt as one point even when far apart) and difficulty judging weights without visual cues (Flournoy experiments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize specific tactile illusions when evaluating touch-based testimony—design tests and controls (visual aid, repeated measures) to detect fused or misleading tactile impressions.
